title: The three-matrix coefficient-minor stability conjecture
statement:
Let $D_1,D_2,D_3$ be positive definite matrices, and let $M$ be the matrix whose entries are the coefficients of $y$ and $z$ in

$$
\det(I+xD_1+yD_2+zD_3).
$$

A minor means the determinant of any finite square submatrix of $M$. **The three-matrix coefficient-minor stability conjecture.** Every minor of $M$ is a stable polynomial in $x$. The source calls this a surprising conjecture and does not establish it.
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0612833

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of December 2006).
source_name: Steve Fisk, “Polynomials, roots, and interlacing”, arXiv:math/0612833 (2008).

progress.label: Open
progress.tldr: A posted calculation claims a concrete counterexample disproves the conjecture in three dimensions, but nobody has independently checked it.
progress.summary:
The conjecture asserts that every coefficient minor arising from three positive definite matrices is stable as a polynomial in $x$. The supplied source describes this as surprising and does not prove it.

**Posted attempt**

A reader-written calculation gives three strictly positive definite $3\times3$ integer matrices and an explicit coefficient minor $\Delta(x)=-4(3076x^3+3012x^2-99x-440)$. Since $\Delta(0)>0$ and $\Delta(1)<0$, it claims a zero $x_0\in(0,1)$, hence a failure of stability and a complete counterexample. The calculation has not been independently verified.

Current status (as of August 2026): A reader-posted counterexample claims to disprove the conjecture, but no independent verification was found, so the conjecture remains mathematically unconfirmed.

*Caveats. The only problem-specific development retrieved is an unverified reader-posted calculation.*

solutions.body:
The conjecture fails already for three strictly positive definite \(3\times3\) integer matrices. Take
\[
D_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&2&0\\
0&0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D_2=
\begin{pmatrix}
13&9&7\\
9&7&5\\
7&5&4
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D_3=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&7&8\\
7&11&12\\
8&12&14
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Their respective lists of leading principal minors are
\[
(1,2,2),\qquad(13,10,2),\qquad(5,6,4).
\]
Hence all three matrices are positive definite by Sylvester's criterion.

Write
\[
M_{ij}(x)=[y^iz^j]\det(I+xD_1+yD_2+zD_3).
\]
The submatrix with row and column indices \(0,1,2\) is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
2x^3+5x^2+4x+1&49x^2+79x+30&28x+22\\
41x^2+65x+24&254x+164&64\\
19x+16&62&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its determinant equals
\[
\Delta(x)
=-4\left(3076x^3+3012x^2-99x-440\right).
\]
But
\[
\Delta(0)=1760>0,
\qquad
\Delta(1)=-22196<0.
\]
The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a real root \(x_0\in(0,1)\). In particular, \(\Delta\) has a zero in the open right half-plane and is not stable.

Thus a coefficient minor of \(\det(I+xD_1+yD_2+zD_3)\) need not be stable, even when every \(D_i\) is strictly positive definite.
